title: Permissions calculator
description: Tick read, write and execute for owner, group and others, and see the `ls -l` letters, the octal mode and the chmod commands change together.
intro: Start with `644`, the usual mode of a new file. Give the group write permission, and watch the second digit go from 4 to 6. Then switch to a directory and read what the same bits mean there. Finally, type `g-w,o=` into the chmod box and predict the result before you run it.
takeaways: The nine letters are three groups of `rwx`: owner, group, others, always in that order. The character before them is the type: `-` for a file, `d` for a directory, `l` for a symbolic link.
Each octal digit adds r = 4, w = 2 and x = 1 for one class, so `rwxr-x---` is `750` and `rw-r--r--` is `644`.
An octal chmod sets every bit at once. A symbolic chmod (`u+x`, `go-w`, `o=`, `a+r`) changes only the bits it names and leaves the rest alone.
On a directory, r lists the names, w creates, deletes and renames entries, and x lets you enter it with `cd` and reach what's inside. Without x, r and w are of little use.

The sticky bit shows as `t` in the last position (`drwxrwxrwt`, octal `1777`, as on `/tmp`). In such a directory, only a file's owner, the directory's owner or root can delete or rename the file. A capital `T` means the sticky bit is set without execute for others.

links.title: inode(7): file type and mode bits, and the sticky bit

file.x: Run it as a program or script.

dir.w: Create, delete and rename entries (together with x).
dir.x: Enter it with cd and reach the entries inside.

sticky.dir: Only a file's owner, the directory's owner or root may delete or rename the files inside, even though others can write to the directory.
sticky.file: Linux ignores the sticky bit on files; it matters on directories.

tasks.text: Ada's script `deploy.sh`: she can read, change and run it, the release group can read and run it, and nobody else can do anything.
tasks.why: Owner rwx (4+2+1 = 7), group r-x (4+1 = 5), others nothing (0).

tasks.text: Jonas's `palette.txt`: he can read and change it, and everyone else can only read it.
tasks.why: rw- is 6 and r-- is 4. This is also what a new file gets with the usual umask 022.

tasks.text: Mira's `passwords.txt`: only she may read and change it.
tasks.why: rw- for the owner and nothing for group and others: 6, 0, 0.

tasks.text: The directory `builds`: the studio group can add and remove builds, everyone else can list and enter it but not change it.
tasks.why: Changing entries needs w and x on the directory; listing and entering need r and x. So rwx, rwx, r-x.

tasks.text: A shared upload directory like `/tmp`: everyone can create files, but nobody can delete someone else's.
tasks.why: rwx for all three classes, plus the sticky bit (the leading 1), which `ls -l` shows as the final `t`.

tasks.text: The directory `private`: Mira has full access, and nobody else can even enter it.
tasks.why: Without x, group and others can't `cd` into the directory or reach anything in it.
